name: Cellulitis
definition: Cellulitis is an infection of the deeper layers of the skin caused by bacteria.
overview: Cellulitis makes the skin painful, hot and swollen, and the area usually looks red, though this may be less obvious on brown or black skin. It can occur on any part of the body, but it is more common on the lower limbs. Bacteria get into the deeper layers of the skin, often through damage such as a scratch or cut. If it is not treated quickly, the infection can spread to other parts of the body, such as the blood, muscles and bones. Early treatment with antibiotics can stop cellulitis becoming more serious.
causes: Bacteria that normally live on the skin surface can enter the deeper tissues through damage such as a spot, scratch or cut.
Streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus are the bacteria most often involved in adults.
Skin conditions such as eczema or athlete's foot can cause small breaks and cracks that let bacteria in.
riskFactors: A weakened immune system, for example because of chemotherapy or diabetes.
Lymphoedema, which is long-term swelling of part of the body.
signs: Skin that is painful, hot, swollen and usually red.
Redness that may be less obvious on brown or black skin.
complications: Spread of the infection to the blood, muscles and bones if it is not treated quickly.
Sepsis, when bacteria reach the bloodstream.
Abscesses, which are collections of pus that may need draining.
Lymphoedema, because cellulitis can damage the lymphatic system.
Necrotising fasciitis, a rare and severe infection that spreads quickly.
diagnosis: A clinician examines the affected area and asks about possible causes. If there are cuts or ulcers in the area, a swab may be taken to identify the bacteria. Because the symptoms overlap with those of a blood clot, further tests may be arranged to rule out a deep vein thrombosis. Diagnosis is usually made from the clinical picture, based on spreading red inflammation of the deeper skin.
treatment: Mild cellulitis affecting a small area of skin is usually treated with antibiotic tablets, usually for about a week. NICE advises oral antibiotics first when the person can take tablets and the condition does not need antibiotics given into a vein. Severe cellulitis may need hospital treatment. Painkillers, raising the affected limb and drinking plenty of fluids help with recovery.
prevention: People at higher risk can help prevent cellulitis by keeping skin conditions such as eczema or psoriasis under control and treating athlete's foot promptly. Maintaining a healthy weight also helps. NICE advises against routine antibiotics to prevent cellulitis coming back, although the NHS says some people with frequent episodes may be prescribed long-term antibiotics.
seekCare: Call 999 or go to A&E for signs of serious complications, such as a very high temperature, a fast heartbeat or breathing, dizziness or fainting, confusion, cold clammy or pale skin, or loss of consciousness. Cellulitis around the eye is treated as urgent. For skin that is painful, hot and swollen, the NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111. The GP should be contacted if there is no improvement 2 to 3 days after starting antibiotics.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of cellulitis?
sections.body:
Cellulitis makes the skin painful, hot and swollen. The area usually looks red, but this may be less obvious on brown or black skin. It can occur on any part of the body, but it is more common on the lower limbs. Some people also feel unwell with flu-like symptoms.

Some NHS trust leaflets describe feeling feverish and shivery for up to 24 hours before any skin changes appear. Symptoms can look worse for the first day or two after treatment starts. Pain and warmth can take longer to settle than the redness, and the redness and warmth can take a couple of weeks to clear completely. The skin may stay darker or change colour after healing, though over time it usually returns to its normal colour. Cellulitis in or around the eye is treated as urgent, and the NHS gives the route to care for this below.

sections.heading: What causes cellulitis and who is more likely to get it?
sections.body:
Cellulitis is an infection caused by bacteria getting into the deeper layers of the skin. The bacteria are usually ones that normally live on the surface of the skin. Damage to the skin, such as a spot, scratch or cut, lets them into the deeper tissues. In adults, the bacteria most often involved are streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus.

The NHS lists poor circulation, a weakened immune system, lymphoedema, injecting drugs, a wound from surgery and having had cellulitis before as risk factors. Skin conditions such as eczema, or a fungal infection of the feet called athlete's foot, can cause small cracks in the skin. Research on lymphoedema suggests it may weaken local immunity and make it harder to clear bacteria. Lymphoedema and cellulitis can each make the other more likely.

sections.heading: How is cellulitis diagnosed?
sections.body:
A clinician examines the affected area and asks about possible causes. If there are cuts or ulcers in the area, the team may take a swab to identify the bacteria. NICE notes that in most cases swabbing of cellulitis gives negative results, especially when the skin is intact. Diagnosis is usually made from the clinical picture, based on spreading red inflammation of the deeper skin.

Because the symptoms overlap with those of a blood clot, the doctor may ask for further tests to rule out a deep vein thrombosis. Other skin conditions, such as venous stasis dermatitis and contact dermatitis, can look like cellulitis. Erysipelas is a related infection that affects the top layers of the skin, while cellulitis reaches deeper tissue. The two can be hard to tell apart, and erysipelas tends to have better-defined edges.

sections.heading: How is cellulitis treated?
sections.body:
For mild cellulitis affecting a small area of skin, a doctor will prescribe antibiotic tablets, usually for about a week. NICE advises oral antibiotics first when the person can take tablets and the condition is not severe enough to need antibiotics given into a vein. If antibiotics are given into a vein, NICE advises a review by 48 hours and a switch to tablets if possible. For infection near the eyes or nose, NICE suggests a different first-choice antibiotic and says specialist advice may be sought.

If cellulitis is severe, the person might be referred to hospital for treatment. The NHS describes painkillers, raising the affected limb, and drinking plenty of fluids as helping with recovery. Some NHS trust leaflets say stopping antibiotics early can allow the infection to return. NHS advice is to contact the GP if there is no sign of feeling better 2 to 3 days after starting antibiotics.

sections.heading: Can cellulitis cause complications or come back?
sections.body:
Serious complications are uncommon, according to NHS trust leaflets. If cellulitis is not treated quickly, the infection can spread to other parts of the body, such as the blood, muscles and bones. Infection that reaches the bloodstream can lead to sepsis, which needs urgent hospital treatment. In severe cases an abscess, a collection of pus, can form and may need draining. Cellulitis can also damage the lymphatic system, which can cause lasting swelling of the affected arm or leg. Necrotising fasciitis is a rare, severe infection of muscle and connective tissue that spreads quickly.

Cellulitis can come back, and this is more likely in people with the risk factors listed above. NICE advises that antibiotics should not be offered routinely to prevent it coming back. The NHS says some people with frequent episodes may be prescribed long-term antibiotics.

sections.heading: When should you get medical help for cellulitis?
sections.body:
The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for skin that is painful, hot and swollen. Call 999 or go to A&E for signs of serious complications. The NHS lists a very high temperature, shivering, a fast heartbeat or breathing, dizziness or fainting, confusion, cold clammy or pale skin, and loss of consciousness. It advises against driving yourself to A&E in this situation.

Cellulitis around the eye is treated as urgent and the NHS describes cellulitis in the eye as very serious. NHS trust leaflets also name redness spreading well beyond the marked area, a red line running up the limb toward the heart, and painful lumps in the groin, armpit or neck as signs of worsening. NICE advises seeking medical help if symptoms worsen rapidly or significantly at any time, or do not start to improve within 2 to 3 days.

faqs.q: How long does cellulitis take to get better?
faqs.a: The NHS says most people make a full recovery after 7 to 10 days. Mild cases are usually treated with antibiotic tablets for about a week. The skin may look worse for the first day or two, and redness and warmth can take a couple of weeks to clear. The GP should be contacted if there is no sign of feeling better 2 to 3 days after starting antibiotics.

faqs.q: What is the difference between cellulitis and erysipelas?
faqs.a: Erysipelas affects the top layers of the skin, while cellulitis affects the deeper layers. Cellulitis tends to have ill-defined borders and develop more slowly, while erysipelas has better-defined borders and develops faster. The two are often hard to separate, and NICE guideline NG141 covers both.

faqs.q: Can cellulitis be mistaken for a blood clot?
faqs.a: The NHS says the symptoms of cellulitis overlap with those of a blood clot. For that reason a doctor may ask for further tests to rule out a deep vein thrombosis. Other skin problems, such as venous stasis dermatitis and contact dermatitis, can also resemble cellulitis.

Cellulitis can come back, and this is more likely in people with risk factors such as poor circulation, a weakened immune system or lymphoedema. The NHS says treating skin conditions such as eczema and athlete's foot may lower the chance of it returning. The NHS says some people with frequent episodes may be prescribed long-term antibiotics. NICE advises against offering antibiotics routinely for this purpose.

faqs.q: When does cellulitis need emergency care?
faqs.a: The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E for signs of serious complications. These include a very high temperature, a fast heartbeat or breathing, dizziness or fainting, confusion, cold clammy or pale skin, and loss of consciousness. Cellulitis in or around the eye is also treated as urgent. Painful, hot and swollen skin that is not an emergency still needs an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111.
